teaching: Kitab al-Mabda' wa'l-Ma'ad by Sayyidna Mu'ayyad is the first book ever written on the subject of origin and return (mabda' wa'l-ma'ad), belonging to the Tayyibi haqa'iq tradition.
Sayyidna Mu'ayyad's famous couplet declares that had he lived in the time of the Prophet Muhammad, his rank would not have been less than that of Salman.
Sayyidna Mu'ayyad authored 800 majalis (sermons) that encompass all the religious sciences.
Sayyidna Mu'ayyad held a very high rank among the bab al-abwab (gate of gates) of the da'wah.
Imam Mustansir gave Sayyidna Mu'ayyad the rank of abu'd-du'at (father of the du'at), to lead the prayers of the du'at; the umm al-du'at (mother of the du'at) is Arwa bint Ahmad, Hurrat al-Malika.
When the a'immah went into concealment, the du'at took over the representation of the Imams; Sayyidna Zu'ayb bin Musa was appointed the first da'i by Mu'ayyad and Hurrat al-Malika.
The prayer of the second day uniquely takes its wasila from the muqatta' Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad, a non-repeating (ghayr-i mukarrar) disjointed-letter group occurring only once in the Quran.

Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad is interpreted as: with Kaf You sufficed (kafayta), with Ha You guided (hadayta), with Ya You made easy (yassarta), with 'Ayn You forgave ('afawta), with Sad You spoke the truth (sadaqta).
Allah has the power to forgive all sins (inna-llaha yaghfiru'dh-dhunuba jami'a).
The Prophet was known as al-Sadiq al-Amin (the truthful, the trustworthy); at the warning of his nearest kindred he presented his hujjat (proof) before announcing his nubuwwat and risalat.
There are two pivotal days in the history of Islam: yawm 'ashirat al-aqrabin (the day of warning the nearest kindred) and the Day of Ghadir.

At the gathering of the kindred, the ten-year-old Ali was the first to say 'Ya Rasulullah' and pledge support; the Prophet declared that whoever supported him would be his khalifa, wasi, and janishin.
On the Day of Ghadir the verse al-yawma akmaltu lakum dinakum was revealed and the Prophet declared man kuntu mawlahu fa-hadha 'aliyyun mawlahu (of whomsoever I am the master, Ali is his master).
Al-Mu'ayyad was a title given by Imam Mustansir (the 18th Imam); his original name was Hibatullah bin Musa bin Sulayman bin Adam al-Shirazi, and his father too was a da'i.
Sayyidna Mu'ayyad was from Shiraz in Iran and later came to Misr (Egypt), where the a'immah and the da'wah were located at that time.
Mufarrij al-Abwab by Sayyidna Ali bin Sulayman is a magnificently arranged collection of the authentic (mustanad) prayers of the Ahl al-Bayt, the Prophet, and Ali.
Sayyidna Mu'ayyad fi'l-Din was from the progeny of the Prophet Sulayman bin Dawud.
Only two prophets passed from mustawda' (temporary abode) to mustaqarr (permanent abode): Idris (of whom it is said wa-rafa'nahu makanan 'aliyya) and Sulayman.

After Sayyidna Muhammad bin Isma'il, the Imams went into concealment; the three concealed Imams (al-masturin al-thalatha) are Ya'la, Ali, and Abu Talib Ali, whose veils (hujub) are 'Abdullah, Ahmad, and Husayn.
In the time of Mawlana Ahmad existed the Rasa'il of the Ikhwan al-Safa.
Sayyidna Mu'ayyad was the hujjat al-'uzma before Imam Mustansir and had many compositions in the zahir, the batin, and the haqa'iq.
Sayyidna Mu'ayyad passed away in the last ten days of Shawwal in 470 Hijri and was buried in the Dar al-'Ilm in al-Qahira al-Mu'izziyya in Egypt.

Mu'ayyad's maternal uncle kept him from the Imam for five years; when he finally reached the Imam he received gnosis and high ranks, and the Imam wrote that if Mu'ayyad's hands were cut off no other Mu'ayyad would be found.
The haqa'iq of Sayyidna Mu'ayyad's du'as were written by Sayyidna Isma'il ibn Muhammad (the Da'i Shumukh) in Kitab al-Subuh; he also authored Mansak al-Hajj.

The book's opening khutba praises Allah, Lord of the worlds, and sends blessings on the Messenger Muhammad the seal of the prophets, his legatee Ali ibn Abi Talib the noblest of legatees, and the Imams of their pure progeny.
Allah described Himself as rabbu'l-'alamin (Lord of the worlds) rather than khaliqu'l-'alamin (creator) because tarbiyat (nurturing) is a higher rank than creation.
The importance of parents derives not from giving birth but from being responsible for upbringing (tarbiyat).
For whichever world Allah is the Lord, the Prophet is its mercy (rahmatan li'l-'alamin).
Allah gave the Messenger such eminence that He made him a partner with Himself in seeing and deciding the deeds of all people (sayara-llahu a'malakum wa-rasuluhu).
Allah, the Knower of the unseen and witnessed ('Alim al-ghaybi wa'sh-shahadah), discloses His unseen to no one except a messenger whom He has chosen (illa man irtada min rasul, Surah al-Jinn).
Allah's pleasure with the Messenger is mentioned in Surah al-Duha (fa-tarda), promising he will be given until he is satisfied.
The Quran from beginning to end is like a qasidah (ode) in praise of the Messenger.
Janab Zaynab taught the haqa'iq of Kaf Ha Ya 'Ayn Sad to women; Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan (Wawaam) will manifest as Mawlatuna Zaynab in the next raj'at.
The treatise is addressed to a pious, rightly-guided brother and answers his question about attaining success and felicity in the ma'ad (hereafter).

The secret of the spiritual malakut connects through revelation with every spiritual rank and reaches the hudud of the sincere ones (mukhlisin), who are charged with taking creatures out of the storm of atoms.

The sincere one (mukhlis) is the secret of the souls and their elixir, illuminating souls and turning them to gold, casting upon them the good color of Allah (Sibghata-llah wa-man ahsanu mina-llahi sibghah).
The sciences of the da'wah, flowing from the hudud and the Imam's gaze, transform the believer's sensual animal soul into a speaking angelic soul (nafs natiqah malakiyyah).

The recipient of these truths is bound by a confirmed, strict covenant ('ahd) of Allah, the same covenant taken from the close angels, the sent prophets, the guiding Imams, and their rightly-guided hudud.
Allah took a covenant and oath of allegiance (bay'at) from the prophets in the Quran, first taking the Messenger's name, then Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, and 'Isa.

The recipient is forbidden to copy or write down the discourse — not a single letter, neither less nor more — to inform anyone except the permitted, and must return the manuscript after finishing reading it.

The Unseen of the Unseen (ghayb al-ghuyub) cannot be comprehended by the mind, encompassed by thought, named, or attributed; the only valid confession is that for all the worlds there is an Originator whom intellects are powerless to comprehend.
Tawhid is the gnosis (ma'rifat) of the higher and lower hudud, not the gnosis of the Exalted Originator, whose gnosis is impossible.
Sayyidna Ja'far bin Sulayman taught that tawhid is not for the Worshipped One but is the gnosis of the hudud (at-tawhid laysa li'l-ma'bud wa-lakin at-tawhid ma'rifat al-hudud).
Without ma'rifat (gnosis of the hudud), one falls into heresy and disbelief (ma'rifat na kuni, zindiqi).
The rank of Sani (the Second) fell from Munba'ith because, though he confessed the Originator and had gnosis of 'Aql al-Awwal, he lacked the gnosis of Munba'ith al-Awwal and claimed to be his equal.
Tawhid requires confessing that every hadd is unique in his rank, with no partner sharing it (kullu haddin minhum wahidun fi rutbatihi).

In the kalima La ilaha illa-llah, among the spiritual intellects only 'Aql al-Awwal is worthy of the name 'Allah'; all others stand at the rank of ilah — just as in our age the higher and lower hudud are at the rank of ilah and only the Imam of the time is at the rank of Allah.

The kalima La ilaha illa huwa is higher than La ilaha illa-llah; it was 'Aql al-Awwal's confession of the Mubdi' (shahida-llahu annahu la ilaha illa huwa), using huwa for the Transcendent Ipseity (al-huwiyyat al-muta'aliyah), whereas the Prophet propagated La ilaha illa-llah.
The numerical (jumal) value of La ilaha illa huwa is 110, as in Surah al-Muzzammil's rabbu'l-mashriqi wa'l-maghribi la ilaha illa huwa fa-ttakhidhhu wakila.

In rabbu'l-mashriqi wa'l-maghribi, the east is Hasan (from whom the Imams rose) and the west is Abu'l-Qasim; all are organized in the being of Ali, and fa-ttakhidhhu wakila commands the Messenger to take Ali as his wasi.
rabbu'l-mashriqayni wa'l-maghribayni (Lord of the two easts and wests) signifies the Imams emerging from Mawlana Ali and ending with him.
Amir al-Mu'minin, in the book Saluni qabla an tafqiduni, exoterically explained the three Quranic forms (one east/west, two, and many) by the sun's rising and setting points across the year.
Tajrid (abstraction) is the stripping of divinity — the power to bring from non-existence to existence — from all originated and created things, and affirming it for their Originator.
Tanzih (transcendence) is the negation of all attributes from the Unseen of the Unseen, confessing that all nobility and majesty, and the divine names, fall upon the First Intellect ('Aql al-Awwal).
Tawhid, tajrid, and tanzih together constitute the essence of what has come from the masters regarding the doctrine of divine unity.
The Unseen of the Unseen originated the world of origination ('alam al-ibda') in a single instant, without time or space — time and space being later creations of the 'Ashir.
The Originator created innumerable luminous forms equal in the first perfection and first existence — life, power, and knowledge — by the requirement of His justice, with no one superior to another.
The intellects themselves ARE the spiritual world ('alam ruhani) and the World of Origination — luminous spirits with no density, no body, contained by no space, and needing no time.

Proof of the intellects' freedom from space and time: our own souls, a tiny part of that world, traverse the distance of east and west and conceive distant heavens and earth in less than the blink of an eye — so how much more for the complete, body-free intellects.

Human intellects are powerless to comprehend the least attribute of the forms of the World of Origination, so they cannot reach a way to comprehend their Originator, who is transcendently higher than all that.

The Indian and non-Arab (Ajami) du'at such as Ali bin Sulayman and Hasan Khan wrote with great clarity, whereas the Arab du'at, despite their high status, made matters obscure; Hasan Khan's 70 haqa'iq books require no dictionary.
To express something easily is harder than to express it obscurely; Sayyidna Hamiduddin al-Kirmani, da'i of the two Iraqs and a bab al-abwab, wrote Rahat al-'Aql clearly yet with deep subtleties.
Excessive grammar is unnecessary for reading the da'wah books; the maxim holds that until a person learns to read without understanding, he can never learn to read Arabic.
Every da'i commanded the people of his island that each marry a female formed in a cave other than his own; the woman formed from a man's own leftover water is like his sister and unlawful to marry.
This marriage rule is declared the pure and exalted path of truth (tariq al-haqq al-tahira al-munazzah).
Guidance belongs to Allah alone (wa ma kunna li-nahtadiya lawla an hadana Allah); Allah told even the Prophet, the greatest guide, that he cannot guide anyone.

The word 'huda' has the numerical value 19 (ha 5, dal 4, ya 10), and the names of the Ahl al-Bayt (Muhammad 4, Ali 3, Fatima 5, Hasan 3, Husayn 4) also total 19, corresponding to the 19 letters of Bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim.
The blessing of the Quran comes from its beginning with Bismillah; therefore the Prophet instructed beginning every act with Bismillah so it will be blessed.
Iyyaka na'budu wa iyyaka nasta'in is a non-repeated phrase occurring only once in the Quran; non-repeated phrases hold greater virtue than repeated ones, and its letters total 19.
Among the muqatta'at, the non-repeated ones (Ya-Sin, Kaf-Ha-Ya-'Ayn-Sad, each once) hold virtue over the repeated ones (Alif-Lam-Mim many times, Ha-Mim seven times).
The verse ihdina's-sirat al-mustaqim is recited 51 times daily, and its letters total 19.
The straight path (sirat al-mustaqim) is the path of those upon whom Allah bestowed favor: the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous (alladhina an'amta 'alayhim).

Birth directly from the earth (clods) occurred only once, in a single first instance at the beginning of the cycle; thereafter procreation between men and women continued until now, and clod-birth will recur at the beginning of the next cycle.
From a single clod only one man and one woman were born — the woman from the man's leftover water and thus his sister — never many individuals.
On Sarandib (Ceylon) 28 clods were formed, and the most excellent among them was that of the juz'i ibda'iya (creative part).
The virtuous person (juz'i ibda'iya) brought forth and appointed his noble son to succeed him in his station, choosing him from his hudud and the people of his mission.
The author states he explained the reality of the beginning explicitly, without symbol or indication (musarrihan fi ghayri ramzin wa-la ishara).
Amir al-Mu'minin taught that a believer should know four things — where he came from, where he will go, how he came, and how he will go — which together constitute the subjects of mabda' and ma'ad.
When the respondent (mustajib) accepts at the hands of a hadd with pure intention toward his hadd and his Sahib al-Zaman, a point of light (nuqta min nur) connects with and neighbors his soul.
Muslim children in believers' houses are only potential believers; they become actual believers at the moment they take the 'ahd-i sharif (noble covenant).

The point of light neighbors the sensual soul without merging with it until death, illuminating and making it radiant; whatever the sensual soul accepts becomes part of the natiqa soul, and what it rejects remains sensual.
Only a small part of the point of light is received per cycle — a portion of the repentance one made in the spiritual world — because the soul cannot bear it in its entirety.

The point of light reaches the believer not directly but through the mediation of his high-ranking hadd; its origin is the substance and flowing support (maddah wa ta'id) from the Exalted Originator (Mubdi' Ta'ala).

The substance and support descends in a chain: from the Mubdi' to the First Preceding Intellect, then to all originating intellects, then to the Tenth, then to every noble station (Natiq, Wasi, or Imam) of the time, then to his higher hudud and downward to the respondent, each receiving according to his worthiness.
Those who take the 'ahd-i sharif do so with differing intentions and receive their portion accordingly.

As the respondent increases in good deeds, establishing the works of shari'ah (the seven pillars), constancy, benefiting from celestial sciences, sincere loyalty (muwalat) to the mawali, and acknowledging each hadd's virtue, his point of light grows, illuminates, and is purified and polished.
All righteous deeds are for the progress of one's own soul, and evil deeds are against it (man 'amila salihan fa-li-nafsihi wa man asa'a fa-'alayha).

The lowest illumination a believer receives is the point of light's illumination upon his sensual soul and body; the natiqa soul is so secretive it does not even inform its neighboring sensual soul (the conscience).

At a believer's last breath his place in paradise is shown to him, causing joy that spreads light on his face; Sayyidna Muhammad bin Fawad al-Qusu (Ghadanfar) carried this radiance his whole life for his services in saving the Da'wah-i Hadiya, and the du'at descend from his lineage until Qiyamah except for four.
Sayyidna Ali bin Sulayman foretold, before the chain of du'at was established, that the du'at would come from the lineage of Sayyidna Muhammad bin Fawad until Qiyamah.

Numerous miracles (mojizaat) are reported of Sayyidna Ali bin Sulayman — the multiplication of food invoking 'Ya Sayyidna Sulayman aghithni', a lost rupee returning upon his head, 500 garments arriving after he gave one away, and his prediction of a man's death by Wednesday — manifesting the blessings of the awliya' Allah's word.

Sayyidna Ali bin Sulayman authored Shu'a' al-Anwar (said to be in daqa'iq rather than haqa'iq) and Anwar al-Shashaniya, and served as da'i for about 35-38 years after the death of Sayyidna Ja'far in 1150.

The luminous form (surah) of the deceased mustajib transfers with each hadd to the one higher than him until it reaches the Bab al-Maqam, the Bab of the Imam of the Time and the greatest servant of the da'wah.

The collection of all luminous forms (suwar) happens at the Bab, not the Imam — analogous to the falak al-buruj gathering all stars while the encompassing falak al-muhit remains empty (bari'); no surah goes to the Imam.
Durud and salam are sent upon the Bab (the fatihu al-kitab) just as upon the Imam.
The luminous forms from all twelve islands (jaza'ir) of the earth gather at the Bab until a luminous structure (haykal nurani) in human form, entirely light, is assembled.

If the haykal nurani appeared to mortals it would dazzle and blind their sight, as no one can look at the sun; it is a spiritual, holy, pre-eternal (azali) light, far greater than the sun's physical light.
The haykal enters the son (farzand) of the Imam and, progressing, will one day become an intellect ('aql).
The Imam does not bestow imamat until the haykal's formation is complete and the ripe suwar gather; very sinful believers who did not repent are held back to be absorbed by the next Imam.
The Bab al-Abwab must also transfer physically (die); for example Mawlatuna Khadijah bint Khuwaylid, the Bab al-Abwab of Fatima, transferred when Mawlana Abu Talib died (three days after).

Each luminous form settles in the haykal according to what it earned in the world — in the position of the heart, brain, eye, ear, hand, foot, hair, nail, or sole — each according to its deed, with no injustice done.

The Bab is so named because the haykal with him is a collection of intellects; since the intellect ('aql) is the essence (lubb) of a life's surah, the Bab is the gatherer of all essences (jami' al-albab).
This haykal is named the Imamah; when the Imam meets the Imamah, the Imam's son goes from potentiality (bil-quwwah) to actuality (bil-fi'l), and then the Imam passes away.
When a believer's soul separates from his body, traces of the vegetative soul (nafs namiyyah) remain as innate heat, also called the winds (riyah).

Of the three souls (namiyyah, hissiyyah, natiqah), the riyah exit fully over three days; those leaving before burial are superior and form the Imam's higher hudud, while those leaving after burial are lower, given the moon's light, and form the Imam's body after purification.

The riyah are purified at the moon, Jupiter, and the sun over 360 years going, 360 returning, and 280 to moderate their temperament — a thousand years total — after which raj'at (return) occurs for all: believer, kafir, munafiq, and Muslim alike.

A believer's three souls unite to form the luminous surah sharif, whereas a kafir, mushrik, or murtadd has no natiqah formed — only namiyyah and hissiyyah manifest in his body, his basest form, and he feels the divine punishment after death.
All souls return after a thousand years; those who fell to the lower realms (darkat) return from there, the da'wah is presented to them, and if they persist they face punishment.
The enemies (azdad) are resurrected in physical form when the Qa'im comes and see the Qa'im as the Imam of their own time — Yazid sees Imam Husayn, Mu'awiyah sees Ali — before the Imam punishes them.
Non-believers are raised with their own imams of misguidance (a'immah al-dalalah, mentioned in the Quran) in the time of the Qa'im.

The windy souls (riyah) fully exit on the third day, which is why Sadaq Allah is recited; good deeds, charity, and prayers within those three days benefit the deceased's body, while later Fatiha gatherings do not.

The purified soul ascends as a subtle vapor to the moon (received by its rays), then via Mercury and Venus to the sun, then to Jupiter; the sun and Jupiter purify the riyah until the suwar at the Bab are complete.

When the Director (Mudabbir) permits the appearance of the Imamic personage, the sun returns the purified windy souls to the moon via Venus and Mercury, and the moon's rays send them to pure water or a noble fruit, descending in a dew drop that only the Imam can attain.
The Prophet said an apple came from Allah, of which he and Khadija each ate half, after which Fatima al-Zahra was born — the same process of the Imamic substance descending in a noble fruit.
The Mudabbir Ta'ala repeatedly mentioned is the 'Ashir, though Hazrat 'Abdullah Sahib held it means the Juz'-i Idayi (Creative Part) of this cycle.

The Imam and his noble, pure wife eat the prepared fruit and unite in marriage, whereupon it becomes a nutfah (sperm-drop) for the Imamic personage, the haykal drawing sustenance from the remaining nourishment.
The mothers of the Imams (Ummahat al-A'immah) are purified (batul) from menstrual blood; though the Imam has several wives, the one from whom his son is born is the batul.

Per Mawla Shaykh Husayn (confirmed by Sayyidna Ali bin Husayn al-Mukarrami), a woman becomes one of the Ummahat al-A'immah as reward for great services rendered as a mansub or da'i in a previous existence, though she returns in female form.
The verse innama yuridu Allahu li-yudhhiba 'ankum al-rijs Ahl al-Bayt wa yutahhirakum tathira praises the Ahl al-Bayt and the Ummahat al-A'immah as far removed from impurity and menstrual blood.
The Imam's son receives nourishment through a nine-month gestation, digesting like an ordinary child, then is born with a noble, camphor-like (kafuri) body made of ru'yah.
The completion of the Bab al-Abwab's surat and the birth of the Imam's son run exactly in parallel (sawa'an bi sawa'an); the Imamah cannot be given until the body's formation is complete.
The Bab passes away and his noble rational soul (nafs natiqah), carrier of all the suwar, connects with the Imam's son; this occurs in a minimum of forty days and a maximum of four years.

As an exception, Mawlana 'Abd al-Muttalib received the haykal from his father Hashim during his mother Salma's pregnancy, before birth, because his station is great as the grandfather of the 'Ayn and the Mim (Ali and Muhammad).

The luminous haykal radiates upon the ghilaf (covering, the Imam's body or nasut); the haykal is the Imamah and the camphor body is the Imam, so the Imam is lower (adna) and the Imamah higher (bar-tar), and their union turns the son from potentiality to actuality.
The Imam's body is called the ghilaf, the shibh kafuri (camphor-like form), and the nasut, while the luminous haykal (collection of suwar) is called the Lahut.

Anwar and asrar are distinct: asrar means the ri'yah and anwar means the suwar; per Sayyidna Ali bin Hiba al-Makrami in Kunuz al-Hikmah, the secrets gathered from the first Da'i Sayyidna Dhu'ayb bin Musa to Sayyidna Sulayman bin Hasan.
There are multiple types of nasut — natural (tabi'i), shadow (dhilli), and special (khas) — and the lawa'ih and lahut vary correspondingly, each nasut being a covering opposite its lahut.

The sensory soul (nafs hissiyah) of the Imam's son carries the luminous haykal and is higher than the rational soul (natiqah) of the Bab, having the power to gather all the suwar — du'at, hujjatayn, mu'minin, ma'dhunin, hudud, and the Bab himself.
The sensory soul of Amir al-Mu'minin was superior to all the lawa'ih of the pure Imams from Mawlana Hunayd to Abu'l-Qasim, except for the three sufara'.

When the father designates (nass) his son for the people of his time, the flowing substance (maddah sariyah) connects to the son through the father and everyone above him up to the First Intellect, an unbroken connection from the corporeal world to the spiritual world.
Through this designation the substance becomes a veil (hijab) and gate (bab) for the son, because the Imam directs his gaze specifically toward him from among the hudud of the world of religion.

The gaze descends in hierarchy: Munba'ith al-Awwal gazed to his Bab, each lower intellect to its veil, and every creative intellect to a hadd of the world of religion, so the substance of guidance flows from top to bottom across the ages.

The designated Imam receives the substance from the hudud until he brings forth his own successor; a Da'i munfarid's very first thought is who his successor will be (awwal al-fikr wa akhir al-'amal — the first thought and the last action).
Ranks are not attained without tests; the da'wah's history is full of trials, and Amir al-Mu'minin declared that Allah tested him fourteen times — seven by the Messenger and seven by Allah.
The Imam brings forth a second son to succeed him in his station, exactly as his own father did before him (sawa'an bi sawa'an, with no difference).

The first Imam, having designated his successor, ascends into the horizon of the Tenth ('ufuq al-'ashir / barzakh-i 'ashiriyyah) and becomes governor of the world (mudabbir al-'alam), while the 'Ashir ascends to a higher rank.

These are partial successorships (juzwi khilafat), not total (kulli); the total successorship of the 'Ashir occurs in one mawr, after which the 'Ashir becomes the Ninth Intellect and progresses upward toward the Munba'ith al-Awwal.

Ten mawrs complete the gathering of the whole realm into intellects congregating at the Munba'ith al-Awwal, leaving only two states: the sphere of the First Intellect (sphere of unity, containing no intellect) and the sphere of the Munba'ith al-Awwal (containing all intellects) — like the empty falak muhit versus the star-filled falak buruj.

When a successor is present, the Da'i appoints no one himself; all rulings flow through the successor (la yunazzilu al-da'i ayya shakhs fi wujud khalifatihi) — illustrated by the nass chains of Ali bin Mawsin al-Shibam, Ghulam Husayn, and Ali bin Sulayman.
Whether a da'i was ghayr-munfarid is known only after his passing; before that he holds the rank of khalifah al-da'i (successor of the Da'i).

The nass chain ran: Ali bin Sulayman to Ibrahim bin Muhammad al-Fahd, whose son Isma'il died in his time, so he designated his nephew Muhammad bin Isma'il, who designated Hasan Khan bin 'Abd al-Malik (who died), then Hibatullah.

Sayyidna Ali bin Hibatullah al-Makrami was the best surah in the congregation of Sayyidna Isma'il bin Hiba, who always sought his intercession in his books; al-Kawakib al-Durriyah was authored in his father's lifetime.

Sayyidna Isma'il bin Hibatullah was eighth in his father's ranking yet designated successor; Hibatullah wrote the tartib (ranking) of his father's hudud, in which the master of the two islands India and Sindh, Sayyidi al-Mansur Karamullah, was the twenty-eighth.

The ascension of the intellects' ranks continues until the third of them reaches the first of the seven intellects in the sphere of the Munba'ith al-Awwal, called hadirat al-quds, which is the final end of the cycles (adwar) and eras (akwar).
No one has access to the rank of the Sabiq al-Awwal (the First Intellect), because it is the rank of unity (rutbat al-wahdah).

When the possessor of the creative body (jussah ibda'iyyah) ascends to the rank of the Tenth after bringing forth his son, he ascends to the horizon of his father, and every Imam after him ascends to him, all remaining in the horizon of the 'Ashir until the Qa'im rises.

The departed pure Imams connect at their Bab, and the Qa'im's Bab al-Abwab is Mawlana Ali, in whom the luminous haykals gathered from Mawlana Hunayd to Abu'l-Qasim (except the three sufara'), across seven cycles of unveiling and seven of concealment.

The sensory soul of Amir al-Mu'minin is the accumulator of the haykals of the Imams of every cycle, uniquely gathering both the previous AND the future Imams (al-awwal wa'l-akhir), unlike any other Imam who gathers only those before him.

A great temple (haykal 'azim) forms for the Bab al-Abwab Ali, every Imam being a limb of it, so that at the Qa'im's hands will be the reckoning (hisab) and reward (thawab) that all previous Imams deferred to him.

The Qa'im brings forth a son from his da'wah and ascends with all the maqamat, which become a single form; the Qa'im's son will be the first Imam of the dawr al-kashf (the second cycle), and is mustaqarr, not mustawda'.
The Qa'im succeeds with the rank of qiyamah; his son is his successor only in the Imamah, not in the rank of qiyamah, for the last Imam of the concealed cycle becomes the next Qa'im.
The coming Qa'im was the successor of the previous cycle's Qa'im, all gathered with Mawlana Ali, so that Ali became the wasi (executor) of the Qa'im.
Sayyidna Isma'il bin Hibatullah states that the Qa'im will have only one son, not two like Mawlana Ali's Hasan and Husayn, and from him the Imamah will continue.

In the dawr al-sitr the Imamah continued not from Hasan but from Husayn; Hasan performed no nass on his son Qasim because Husayn was an infallible born one (mawlud ma'sum) already designated by the Prophet.
Designation (nass wa tawqif) is obligatory; the Prophet performed nass on Hasan and Husayn, and Mawlana Ali confirmed the Prophet's will at the end of his life (akkada wasiyyat Rasulillah).
Hasan is subsumed within Husayn (al-Hasanu fi al-Husayn) — Hasan is present within Husayn, even within the letters of his name.
Upon the Qa'im's hands will be the reckoning (hisab), the reward (sawab), and the punishment (iqab) — the major decisions of the resurrection.
The Qa'im's veil (hijab/occultation) will not last more than three days because his are the highest riyahat, which cannot remain longer in the world; then he appoints his son.
The Qa'im has a new glory each day (kullu yawmin huwa fi sha'n), being the essence of all cycles (adwar) and spheres (akwar), since all the stations of the Pure Imams consolidate in him.
The Qa'im's likeness is like an intellect of the World of Origination, and he succeeds the Tenth in his rank — a partial successorship (khilafat juzwi), not total.

The Qa'im manages the world through substance (maddah) and support (ta'id) in a partial management, and the stations transfer to his horizon, one imam after another, until the second Qa'im of the resurrection rises.

In the dawr al-kashf a Qa'im rises every thousand years, so 47,000 years yield 47,000 Qa'ims; the seventh gathers the previous six (7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42), and the 47,000-year Qa'im is the true Qa'im of the dawr al-kashf of most magnificent glory.
Mawlana Hunaid gathers the remaining 3,000 years of the dawr al-fatrat, as Sayyidna Ali bin Sulayman mentioned that the Qa'im of the dawr al-kashf gathered 47,000 years (not 50,000).
Known history extends only from Adam; what came before was deliberately erased from human minds by the da'wah's will, and science describes earlier artifacts only partially (juzwi), not completely.

This esoteric knowledge came through ta'id and is all implicitly present in the Quran (kashf, sitr, adwar, akwar are not explicit but are contained there); per Ghulam Husayn Sahib, the Quran is the true source and repository, and the Dawoodi sciences agree up to Sayyidna Burhanuddin.

The total dawr al-kashf spans 50,000 years (47,000 pure kashf plus 3,000 fatrat); at its end evil increases and good decreases, so it is resolved that the haqa'iq be cut off and concealed after having been openly manifest, recited on the minbar and in gatherings.
After concealment, the haqa'iq reach only the one who seeks them from their proper doors (abwab) through covenants ('uhud) and strict pledges (mawathiq).

The dawr al-sitr begins with Adam, the first of the nuqata'; Nuh, who came after, was the first of the Ulul-'Azm and brought a new shari'ah, whereas Adam is a nuqata' but not Ulul-'Azm (lam najid lahu 'azma).
Each subsequent natiq — Ibrahim, Musa, 'Isa, and Muhammad — brought a new shari'ah abrogating that of his predecessor.

The cycles of the prophets correspond to stages of embryonic creation relative to the awaited Qa'im: Adam's cycle is the shadow (zill), Nuh's the drop (nutfah), Ibrahim's the clot ('alaqah), Musa's the lump (mudghah), 'Isa's the bones ('izam), and Muhammad's the flesh (lahm) — hence the Prophet's love of meat.

Sayyidna Ali bin Sulayman in Jinan al-Jinan demonstrated that the three 'ulama of the era (Sulayman bin Hasan, Muhammad bin Fahd, Ja'far bin Sulayman) are the essence of the du'at, the letters of their names coinciding with those of the hudud of every cycle from Adam onward.

Anecdote: the narrator's letter-matching of the hudud of Sayyidna Husayn bin Hasan was corrected by Sayyidna, who knew which figures truly were among his hudud and which were not (e.g. Abdullah was a mansub, Muhsin Shayba was not), illustrating that a believer sees with the light of Allah.
Every maqam — natiq, wasi, or imam — from Adam to the last Imam of Muhammad's cycle, upon transferring, settles in the horizon of the Tenth and manages the world of nature, until Abu al-Qaim is born.
The last Imam of Muhammad's cycle is the Qa'im al-qiyamah; all who transferred from Adam to him connect with him, his noble soul becoming their carrier, and all become a single luminous form.
The Qa'im appears with his hujjah preceding him in the da'wah; this hujjah is the Mahdi of the End of Time, who comes before the Qa'im.

It is among the possibilities that the Qa'im (if the present Imam is Abu al-Qaim) has already been born; his birth from the Ka'ba is not established (unlike Mawla Ali's), and he is muhayyir al-rutbah (one who confounds the ranks).

Sayyidna Idris bin Hasan in Subur al-Sabi' states that when the Qa'im rises his age will be 37 — the number of times 'La ilaha illa Allah' occurs in the Quran (37 times across 36 verses in five different forms).

La ilaha illa Anta is the only non-repeated form, occurring once in the Quran in the supplication of the prophet Yunus (la ilaha illa anta inni kuntu min az-zalimin), to which Allah responded instantly (fa-istajabna lahu), and thus the believers too are saved.

Allah gives the hujjah possession of the entire earth and compels obedience: he loses the first battle (the Romans win), wins the second, and the seven continents come under his control; when he declares himself a servant of the Qa'im the people turn away, and then the great gathering (hashr) occurs.

The hujjah proclaims in all horizons that whoever chooses a religion may adhere to it and be safe, so everyone manifests his belief; with the appearance of falsehood (batil), the matter becomes severe for the people of truth.
Sayyidna Husayn (a sutrah of the qiyamah) taught that the Qa'im appears with knowledge and the sword both, and indicated that the entire reality of the qiyamah is contained within Surah al-Fatiha.

Surah al-Fatiha has seven verses and 25 words, corresponding to the 25 prophets named in the Quran and indicating the Imam's system: 12 daytime hudud (in the islands), 12 nighttime hudud (in his presence), and the Imam himself as the 25th.

Sayyidna Hasan bin Hamid bin Malik holds that Surah al-Fatiha encodes the number of Imams via 'hamd' (ha 8 + mim 40 + dal 4 = 52): 49 Imams from Hasan to Abu al-Qaim plus the Prophet, Ali, and Fatima, after which the qiyamah occurs.

The qaim al-qiyamah appears suddenly (baghtatan); all creation from all horizons gathers, and the first and the last are assembled at the appointed time (innal-awwalina wal-akhirina la-majmu'una ila miqati yawmin ma'lum) — the known day being the Qa'im and the miqat their place of meeting with him.

Before the Qa'im, every imam, hadd, believer, and their opposites (azdad) take form; he makes them aware of their deeds and commands the believers to slaughter all the azdad as at Mina, after which a fire descends from the sky to burn them before they descend to the greater punishment of Sijjin/Saqar in the lowest earth.

Punishment is of three types: the nearer ('adhab adna, the rah khunnar of seven levels), the intermediate ('adhab awsat, ice within the poles and mountains), and the greater ('adhab akbar, Saqar — the most severe, where the azdad of the da'wah are kept for one great cycle, punished by the moon's light by day and the sun's by night, killed and revived a thousand times nightly, neither dying nor living).

The 'known day' (yawm ma'lum) gathering is for those in the da'wah; the opposites of Adam, Nuh, and the rest come in human form and are punished through the believers by the Qa'im, while many who are not opposites are spared.

After the judgment the Qa'im appoints his son caliph, ascends with all the maqamat under his charge, becomes caliph of the Tenth, and proceeds with his son for the 50,000 years of the dawr al-kashf, which alternates between unveiling (kashf) and concealment (sitr).

There are three cycles: the pure dawr al-kashf (founded upon haqa'iq), the dawr al-fatrat (founded upon ta'wil, 3,000 years of sluggishness), and the dawr al-sitr (founded upon shari'ah, 7,000 years); the fatrat, though at the end of the kashf, is counted within the dawr al-sitr.
Mawlana Ali said that every 10,000 years a form appears and that form is him, combining the 3,000 years of fatrat and the 7,000 years of sitr.

Every maqam — prophet, wasi, or imam — is connected to the substance from the First Intellect perpetually, without interruption for even the blink of an eye, as the Quran says la ta'khudhuhu sinatun wa la nawm (neither slumber nor sleep overtakes Him), meaning neither complete nor partial inattention.
